text: The capstone: writing a real architecture decision record. This closing lesson asks you to do the thing this entire course has been building toward -- given a real, unresolved decision at Northbeam, write your own ADR, scoring the trade-offs honestly, accounting for build-versus-buy, and writing it in the structure this course taught, before checking your answer against a model ADR.

Here's the scenario. Northbeam's support assistant currently answers every question it attempts, even when retrieval found only weak, low-relevance matches -- which sometimes produces confidently-stated wrong answers. Leadership wants a decision: should the team add a confidence threshold that routes low-confidence answers to a human agent instead? Two real options are on the table. Option A, a static threshold: one fixed relevance-score cutoff, simple to implement and explain, but it may not generalize well across different question types. Option B, a learned threshold: a small classifier trained on historical outcome data, more accurate in principle, but it requires labeled data Northbeam may not fully have yet, and is itself a new model to build and maintain. Before moving on, write your own ADR using Context, Decision, Consequences, and Alternatives Considered.

Here's the model answer's decision. Start with a static threshold, tuned against a small manually-labeled sample of recent real answers, and revisit a learned-classifier approach once the static-threshold period itself has accumulated enough labeled outcome data. Option A isn't a dead end here -- it's actual preparation for Option B.

The consequences are stated honestly on both sides. On the positive side: it ships quickly with no new model to validate or maintain, and the static period generates exactly the labeled data a future classifier would need. On the negative side: a single fixed cutoff won't generalize equally well across all question types, and it will need manual re-tuning if patterns shift. The alternatives get the same honesty -- a learned classifier from day one is rejected for now because the labeled data doesn't exist yet to train or validate it reliably, and no threshold at all is rejected because that's the actual problem this ADR exists to solve.

If you proposed going straight to a learned classifier because you assumed Northbeam already had enough historical data, that's a completely legitimate, defensible call -- the point of this exercise isn't matching the model answer's conclusion exactly, it's reasoning the way the model answer reasons: naming the real trade-off, being honest about what's unknown, and writing the decision down so it can be understood and challenged later. That's also exactly why "walk me through how you'd decide X" is one of the most common Staff and Principal interview formats -- it tests whether you can structure an ambiguous decision and communicate the reasoning clearly, not just arrive at an answer.

That closes this course. You started by learning to build the thing correctly. You're finishing by owning the decision behind it, the incident when it breaks, the standard that keeps a team aligned, the call on when debt is worth paying down, and the roadmap that turns a business goal into sequenced technical work. That combination -- technical judgment plus the ownership to carry it through a team, an incident, and a plan -- is the real difference between a senior engineer and an architect-level technical leader. You're ready to lead.
